summary: This note surveys the early coinage of India and one later phase of it. It states that the first Indian coins were punch-marked silver pieces minted around the 6th century BCE by the Mahajanapadas of the Indo-Gangetic Plain, before Alexander the Great's invasion. It describes their symbols, weight standard and irregular shape. It also notes that the Gupta Empire produced large numbers of gold coins showing kings performing rituals, and silver coins influenced by the earlier Western Satraps under Chandragupta II.
one_line: Overview of India's coinage, from early punch-marked silver coins of the Mahajanapadas to Gupta Empire gold and silver issues.
key_facts: The first coins in India were minted around the 6th century BCE by the Mahajanapadas of the Indo-Gangetic Plain.
The first Indian coins were minted certainly before the invasion of Alexander the Great in the 4th century BCE.
Early Indian coins of this period were punch-marked coins called Puranas, Karshapanas or Pana.
Saurashtra's punch-marked coins had a single symbol, a humped bull.
Dakshin Panchala's punch-marked coins had a Swastika as their symbol.
Magadha's punch-marked coins had several symbols rather than a single one.
Early Indian coins were made of silver of a standard weight but had an irregular shape.
The irregular shape arose from cutting up silver bars and then cutting the edges of the coin to reach the correct weight.
The Gupta Empire produced large numbers of gold coins depicting the Gupta kings performing various rituals.
The Gupta Empire produced silver coins clearly influenced by those of the earlier Western Satraps.
The Gupta silver coinage influenced by the Western Satraps was produced by Chandragupta II.
